q: What are the main sights in Bihać?
a: The main sights in central Bihać are Kapetanova kula (the Captain's Tower) with its museum, the Fethija Mosque, the ruins of St Anthony of Padua's church with its tall tower, and the turbe (Ottoman mausoleum), all close to one another. Nearby you will find Sokolac fortress, Japodski otoci (the Japod Islands) in Račić and Ostrožac near Cazin. On top of that, the town itself, set on the islands and rapids of the Una, is one of the most beautiful sights in Bihać.

q: How old is the town of Bihać?
a: Bihać is first mentioned on 26 February 1260 in a charter of the Hungarian-Croatian king Béla IV. Two years later, in 1262, Béla IV granted it the status of a free royal town. The area was settled much earlier, in the time of the Japodes, an Illyrian people who lived along the Una in the first millennium BC.

q: What is Kapetanova kula (the Captain's Tower) in Bihać?
a: Kapetanova kula is a stone tower in the centre of Bihać and one of the oldest surviving buildings in the town. It is named after the town captain who lived on the top floor, and in Austro-Hungarian times and later it served as a prison. In 1972 it was turned into a museum, and its most recent restoration was completed in 2021.

q: When was the Captain's Tower in Bihać built?
a: The exact date the Captain's Tower (Kapetanova kula) was built is not known, and historians disagree: some place it in the Middle Ages, others in the early Ottoman period. What is certain is that it was part of the old Bihać fortress and for centuries served a defensive and later a prison role. Today it houses a museum on the history of the region.

q: What can you see in the Captain's Tower museum in Bihać?
a: The Captain's Tower (Kapetanova kula) houses several permanent exhibitions covering the period from prehistory to the Austro-Hungarian era. One floor presents the spiritual and material culture of the Japodes, another the ancient towns of Una-Sana Canton, and at the top the captain's divanhana (a traditional reception room) has been recreated. From the top of the tower there is a view over the old town and the Una.

q: What are the opening hours of the Captain's Tower museum?
a: The museum in the Captain's Tower (Kapetanova kula) is usually open on weekdays in the morning and early afternoon, for shorter hours on Saturdays, and is mostly closed on Sundays. Opening hours and ticket prices may change, especially outside the season. Before your visit, check the latest information with the Museum of Una-Sana Canton. The tower is in the old part of town, a few steps from the Fethija Mosque.

q: What is the Fethija Mosque in Bihać?
a: The Fethija Mosque in Bihać was originally the Catholic church of St Anthony of Padua, built in 1266 in the Gothic style. After the Ottoman conquest of Bihać in 1592 it was converted into a mosque and named Fethija, meaning 'conquest'. It is considered one of the oldest Gothic buildings in Bosnia and Herzegovina and is a protected national monument.

q: Why does the Fethija Mosque in Bihać look like a church?
a: The Fethija Mosque looks like a church because that is what it originally was: the Gothic church of St Anthony from the 13th century, converted into a mosque in 1592. Its Gothic windows, portal and rose window have survived, which is rare among mosques. The old Gothic bell tower served as a minaret until 1863, when it was demolished because of its poor condition and replaced with a new minaret.

q: Can tourists visit the Fethija Mosque?
a: Fethija is an active mosque and can generally be viewed from the outside, while going inside depends on prayer times and permission. A full restoration was announced at the beginning of 2026, so the interior may be closed for a period. If you go in, dress modestly and take off your shoes; women usually cover their hair with a scarf.

q: What remains of St Anthony's church in the centre of Bihać?
a: What remains of the Catholic church of St Anthony of Padua in the centre of Bihać is its tall tower and parts of the walls. The church was completed at the end of the 19th century and destroyed in the bombing of 1943, when much of the town centre was hit. The ruin stands next to the Captain's Tower and the Fethija Mosque and is one of the most recognisable sights in Bihać.

q: Is the tall tower in the centre of Bihać part of the Fethija Mosque?
a: The tall tower in the centre of Bihać belongs to the ruins of the later Catholic church of St Anthony of Padua, built under Austro-Hungarian rule and destroyed in 1943. It is not the bell tower of Fethija: Fethija is the old Gothic church from 1266, now a mosque with a minaret. Both buildings are named after St Anthony, so visitors often confuse them.

q: What is the turbe in Bihać?
a: The turbe in Bihać is a small Ottoman tomb, a mausoleum, in the town centre next to the Captain's Tower and the Fethija Mosque. Together they form the historic core of the old town. It is viewed from the outside, and a tour of all these sights together takes less than an hour. It is best seen as part of a walk around the old town.

q: When did the Ottomans conquer Bihać?
a: The Ottomans conquered Bihać in June 1592, after a siege lasting about ten days. The town then remained an important Ottoman fortress on the border with the Habsburg Monarchy for almost three centuries. It was then that St Anthony's church was converted into the Fethija Mosque.

q: When did Bihać become part of Austria-Hungary?
a: Ottoman rule in Bihać ended in 1878, after the Congress of Berlin, when Austria-Hungary took over the administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During this period the town gained new public buildings, the Catholic church of St Anthony and more modern streets. The Captain's Tower was turned into a prison at that time.

q: What was AVNOJ and what is its connection to Bihać?
a: AVNOJ was the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia, whose First Session was held in Bihać on 26 and 27 November 1942. At the time the town was under Partisan control, a period known as the Bihać Republic. The Second Session of AVNOJ was held a year later, on 29 and 30 November 1943, in Jajce.

q: What was the Bihać Republic?
a: The Bihać Republic is the name for a large area held by the Partisans in late 1942 and early 1943, centred on Bihać. The town was liberated in early November 1942, and the First Session of AVNOJ was held there on 26 and 27 November. The area was abandoned at the end of January 1943 in the face of a German offensive.

q: Is there an AVNOJ museum in Bihać?
a: The former Museum of the First Session of AVNOJ was merged with the town museum in 1964, and its collection is now part of the Museum of Una-Sana Canton in Bihać. The museum has history, archaeology, ethnology and art departments. For current exhibitions and opening hours, contact the museum directly.

q: Who were the Japodes?
a: The Japodes were an Illyrian people who lived roughly in the last millennium BC across the wider area of the middle Una, in today's Lika, Gorski kotar and part of Slovenia. They built settlements along the river and fished, and were later conquered by the Romans. Their graves, amber jewellery and decorated urns have been found around Bihać.

q: Where were the Japodian urns found?
a: The Japodian urns are decorated stone vessels for the ashes of the dead, found in necropolises around Bihać; the first was discovered in 1890 at the Jezerine necropolis. They are decorated with figures of people and animals and date from around the 5th century BC to the Roman period. The most important finds are kept in museums in Sarajevo, and some Japodian material is also on display in Bihać.

q: What are the pile dwellings at Ripač?
a: At Ripač, about 5 km from Bihać, remains of a prehistoric settlement of pile dwellings have been found: wooden houses built over the river on oak posts driven into the riverbed. Settlements like this are rare in the Balkans and in Europe. Ripač is on the way to Una National Park, so it fits easily into a trip along the river.

q: What is Japodski otoci (the Japod Islands) near Bihać?
a: Japodski otoci is a leisure spot in Račić near Bihać, on several river islands in the Una connected by footbridges, on the edge of Una National Park. They are named after the Japodes, and sculptures depicting them stand on the islands. There is a restaurant, accommodation, footpaths and a rafting launch point, and they are about 15 km from the centre of Bihać.

q: What is Sokolac fortress near Bihać?
a: Sokolac is a medieval fortress on a hill above the village of the same name, a few kilometres south of Bihać, on the road to Una National Park and Štrbački buk. It is first mentioned at the end of the 14th century and has been declared a national monument of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After restoration it opened to visitors in 2015, and from it you can see Bihać and the Una valley.

q: How do I get to Sokolac fortress from Bihać?
a: Sokolac fortress is about 5 km south of the centre of Bihać, reached by car on the road towards Una National Park or on foot via a hiking trail in about an hour. From the car park it is a short climb to the top. If you are staying in Lohovo, Sokolac is on your way to Štrbački buk.

q: What is Ostrožac Castle?
a: Ostrožac is a fortress and castle above the Una river near Cazin, about 17 km north of Bihać. It was built in several phases: a 13th-century medieval fortress, an Ottoman section and a castle rebuilt between 1900 and 1906 by Lothar von Berks. The courtyard contains a park with more than 150 stone sculptures, and the complex has been a national monument since 2013.

q: Who was Lothar von Berks?
a: Lothar von Berks was an Austro-Hungarian administrator of Bihać who, at the start of the 20th century, between 1900 and 1906, remodelled Ostrožac Castle near Cazin. According to local tradition, he restored the castle as a gift for his wife. Thanks to this remodelling, Ostrožac today looks like a romantic castle rather than just a fortress.

q: What is the sculpture colony at Ostrožac?
a: For more than half a century, a sculpture colony has been held in the courtyard of Ostrožac, where sculptors carve works from bihacit, a local stone. More than 150 sculptures have remained in the courtyard, creating an open-air sculpture park. The sculptures are an integral part of the protected national monument.

q: Was Bihać under siege during the 1990s war?
a: Yes, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina Bihać was under siege for about three years, from 1992 to 1995. The siege ended in August 1995. Today the town has been rebuilt and is peaceful, and memorials in the town bear witness to that period.

q: What is the population of Bihać?
a: According to the 2013 census, the City of Bihać had around 56,000 inhabitants, of whom about 43,000 lived in the urban area itself. Bihać is the seat of Una-Sana Canton and the largest town on the Una river. It lies at roughly 230 m above sea level. The Una flows through the town and gives it its distinctive character.

q: Why is Bihać built on islands?
a: The Una flows through Bihać in several channels, around islands and over small cascades, so part of the town is built on river islands. In the oldest charter, from 1260, Bihać is mentioned as a town on the island of St Ladislaus. These channels and bridges still give the town centre its special character.

q: Can I explore the old town of Bihać on foot?
a: Yes, the historic centre of Bihać with the Captain's Tower, the Fethija Mosque, the ruins of St Anthony's church and the turbe can be explored on foot in one to two hours, including a walk along the Una. Everything is close together and on flat ground. If you stay in one of our apartments in the centre, the old town is just a few minutes' walk away.

q: Was Bihać a free royal town?
a: Yes, King Béla IV declared Bihać a free royal town in 1262, under the direct authority of the Hungarian-Croatian crown. According to local tradition, the king took refuge in Bihać from the Tatars and rewarded the town with privileges. Throughout the Middle Ages Bihać was an important centre of the Croatian kingdom.

q: Are there Roman remains in Bihać?
a: Yes, the area of Una-Sana Canton has remains of ancient settlements and Roman finds, some of which are displayed in the exhibition on ancient towns in the Captain's Tower. The Romans conquered the Japodes and incorporated this region into their province. There are not many visible Roman buildings in Bihać itself, so the museum is the best place to learn about that period.

q: What is the oldest building in Bihać?
a: The oldest reliably dated building in Bihać is the Fethija Mosque, formerly the Gothic church of St Anthony from 1266. The Captain's Tower is also very old, but its exact age has not been established. Both are in the very centre of town, a few steps from each other.

q: What is Ostrovica fortress near Kulen Vakuf?
a: Ostrovica is a medieval and Ottoman fortress on a hill above Kulen Vakuf, in the south of the Bihać area on the Una. It offers a wide view over the Una valley and the village below. A steep path leads up to it, so bring good footwear and water.

q: Is Ripač historically significant?
a: Ripač is historically significant as the site of a prehistoric Japodian pile-dwelling settlement and as a medieval fortress that the Habsburgs defended against the Ottomans in the 16th century. Today it is a village on the Una on the way from Bihać to Una National Park. Its riverside restaurants make it a pleasant place for a short stop.

q: What role did Bihać play in the Second World War?
a: Bihać played a special role in the Second World War because the First Session of AVNOJ, the foundation of the future Yugoslav federation, was held there in November 1942. The town was heavily damaged by bombing, particularly in 1943, when St Anthony's church was also destroyed. This part of its history is presented in the Museum of Una-Sana Canton.

q: How long do I need to see the sights of Bihać?
a: Half a day is enough for central Bihać with the Captain's Tower, the Fethija Mosque and a walk along the Una. If you add Sokolac and Japodski otoci you will need a full day, and with Ostrožac and Štrbački buk, two days. q: Are there guided tours of Bihać?
a: Guided tours of Bihać are occasionally organised through local travel agencies and the tourist board, especially in the season. What is on offer and prices change, so check in advance. q: What is the Bihać brewery (Bihaćka pivovara)?
a: Bihaćka pivovara is the local brewery known for Preminger beer, which is served in most cafés and restaurants in town. Industrial beer production in Bihać has a long tradition and is part of the town's identity. The easiest way to try it is at any café by the Una.

q: Is Ostrožac Castle open to visitors?
a: Ostrožac can be visited, and the courtyard with its sculpture park is usually open to visitors, while some parts of the castle are being restored. The town of Cazin has secured funding to restore Lothar von Berks's castle, so visiting conditions may change. Before setting off, check the current situation with the Cazin tourist board or the town of Cazin.
